You've moved up to probability bounds and equally likely outcomes. Here is the ground we'll stand on. A probability is a number between zero and one, with zero for an impossible event and one for a certain event; everything else lives in between, and no event can have a probability outside that range. That single fact gives you a free error check on every answer you ever write. Next, equally likely outcomes have equal probability. When a coin is fair or a spinner's sections are the same size, each outcome takes an equal share of the total, so a probability becomes a matter of counting: how many outcomes belong to the event, compared with how many outcomes there are altogether. If outcomes were not equally likely, counting them would mislead you, so always ask whether the equal-share assumption really holds before you count. In the problems ahead, you will be told the two counts; your job is to put the favorable count over the total count and to check that the result respects the bounds.
